Leave-one-out cross-validation for a fit

Source: R/loo.R
fit_loo.Rd

Computes the expected log pointwise predictive density with Pareto-smoothed importance sampling (or WAIC), leaving out one individual at a time. Animal fits with missing trait records are supported.

Usage

fit_loo(
  x,
  criterion = c("loo", "waic"),
  r_eff = NULL,
  unit = c("individual", "record"),
  eigen_A = NULL,
  transform = NULL,
  ...
)

# S3 method for class 'CmdStanMCMC'
loo(x, ...)

# S3 method for class 'stanfit'
loo(x, ...)

Arguments

x

A fit object.

criterion

"loo" for Pareto-smoothed importance sampling, or "waic" for the widely applicable information criterion.

r_eff

Relative effective sample sizes, one per observation. Computed from the within-chain correlation of the pointwise likelihoods when left NULL, which is what relative_eff recommends.

unit

For animal fits, what one pointwise term is. "individual" (default) leaves out one individual: the term is the density of its observed traits given every other individual, computed after the fit from the draws of G, E, beta and, with gaps, Y_mis. "record" uses the model's own log_lik, one term per record rotated by the eigenvectors of A, which needs a complete response. Ignored for phenotypic fits and draws matrices, whose terms are already one per individual or are taken as given.

eigen_A

Optional eigendecomposition of the relationship matrix the fit used (attr(fit, "stanimal_data")$A, after any reordering and blend_A), as a list with Q and lambda, to skip the \(O(N^3)\) decomposition for unit = "individual". It is checked against that matrix.

transform

Optional size_shape object, when x was fitted to its scores. The terms are then moved to the original traits, so the result can be compared with a fit to those traits (see Details).

...

Further arguments passed to loo or waic, such as k_threshold or cores.

Value

An object from the loo package: a psis_loo or waic object. loo_compare() accepts several of them, which is how fits are compared; the differences in ELPD are what matters, not the absolute value. For unit = "individual", the attribute "units" names the individual of each pointwise term, so a high Pareto \(k\) can be traced to an animal.

Details

Relatives share breeding values, so an animal model does not factorize over individuals and the density of one animal depends on all the others. The default terms are those of leave-one-out for a non-factorized normal model (Bürkner, Gabry and Vehtari 2021): for each draw, the conditional density of an individual's observed traits given every other individual, with that individual's own gaps integrated out. When other individuals have gaps, the draw conditions on their sampled values (Y_mis), which keeps the importance sampling exact. Individuals with no observed trait carry no term. The cost per draw is two \(N \times N\) by \(N \times K\) matrix products, batched over draws, plus one decomposition of A.

Phenotypic models use one term per individual, integrating missing traits out, from their own log_lik.

With unit = "record", the terms are the animal model's log_lik: for complete responses they sum to the joint log likelihood, but the rotation mixes individuals, so a term is not one animal left out. That criterion is refused for responses with gaps, whose log_lik terms use imputed values.

Compare fits to the same response values, observations and missingness pattern, with the same unit. The terms are densities of the standardized response, so the absolute ELPD carries a constant that depends on the data's scale; it cancels in comparisons between fits to the same response. Individual-level terms assume the built-in likelihood and are refused for a custom model_file. If response or model metadata are unavailable (a bare draws matrix or an older fit), the model's log_lik is used with a warning: the caller must verify that its terms are suitable predictive units. Extracting raw draws and passing them directly to loo::loo() or loo::waic() bypasses these checks.

Fits to size and shape scores. The scores of size_shape are the same linear map of every individual's traits, \(s = M y + c\). Conditioning on the other individuals' scores is conditioning on their traits, so a term of the score fit becomes the term of the traits by the Jacobian \(|\det M|\), a constant, together with the change from the scores' standard deviations to the traits'. transform adds that constant to every term, and loo_compare() can then set a fit to the scores against a fit to the traits. The constant leaves the Pareto \(k\) values and the standard error of a difference unchanged. It needs a complete response (gaps are filled before the rotation, so the scores are not a function of the observed data) and every shape axis (with fewer, \(M\) is not invertible). The shape axes are principal components of the data, including the individual left out; that touches the prior and not the likelihood, and with more than a few dozen individuals it is negligible. The result carries attr(, "scale") = "traits".

References

Bürkner, P.-C., Gabry, J. and Vehtari, A. (2021). Efficient leave-one-out cross-validation for Bayesian non-factorized normal and Student-t models. Computational Statistics 36, 1243–1261. doi:10.1007/s00180-020-01045-4

See also

posterior_predictive

Examples

if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{
fit1 <- lmm_animal(Y, X, A)
fit2 <- lmm_animal(Y, X, A, genetic_structure = "factor", n_factors = 2)
loo::loo_compare(fit_loo(fit1), fit_loo(fit2))

# raw traits against size and shape scores
ss <- size_shape(Y)
fit3 <- lmm_animal(ss$scores, X, A)
loo::loo_compare(fit_loo(fit1), fit_loo(fit3, transform = ss))
} # }
